The feedback problem is mostly because you can't really know what you need until you need it, with such large websites.

The time problem, on the other hand, is a pretty impossible one to solve : there is a minimum amount of time needed to write tools that integrate well in the current codebase, are well tested and secure. ( and adding an infinite amount of devs doesn't work, so there's really no real way to avoid that problem )

Imagine you have 50 000 pieces of Lego. You build a castle that's 2 meter high and covers an area of 4 square meters, with stables and courtyards and whatnot. After a while you decide that you want to make the king's hall bigger. That requires you to take apart some part of the castle away, without collapsing the walls around the king's hall and without ripping out all of the other parts. It sounds easy, but surgical precision* is needed for this task.

Similarly, if you want to change the functionality of an existing piece of software, you have to be careful not to break existing functionality or introduce new bugs. In theory it's easy, in practice multiple modules can depend on one another and changing one might break others.

As to what the mod tools are, no idea, didn't moderate anything, but it does seem that they're a big enough deal to be used as a smoke screen and damage control tool

* = exaggeration

Now imagine most of the walls of the castle are actually invisible, so you're having to rely on hastily-drawn sketches of where the original architect thought they might end up eventually, and you might not even know you've broken one until five thousand Huns show up in the courtyard.

And also imagine your boss doesn't really understand what you're doing, either, and just keeps telling you to do it faster and cheaper, and the people that live in the castle keep yelling that you're lazy and stupid.
Oh, and there are parts that sit on top of each other, but instead of being connected by studs they slide on one another.

If everything is done right, inserting new modules shouldn't be hard. The problem is that sometimes you need to cut corners due to time or budget constraints. And one corner that you might cut is writing a function that tells you the color of a circle. But instead of making it so that it will tell you the color of an arbitrary shape (which a circle might be), you write it specifically for circles. And later on you need to know the color of a square. Now you have to modify that function to make it either accept squares as well, or modify it such that it accepts any shape. This is a very simplified example obviously.

Some extra time should be spent analyzing and predicting future features before actually implementing something, because it might come and bite you in the ass later on and delay the release of whatever you're working on.
